questions.question: How is memory managed in Java? Explain Heap, Stack, String Pool, Memory Leak, StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError.
questions.answer:
In Java, memory is managed by the JVM (Java Virtual Machine). Whenever we run a Java application, the JVM allocates memory to store objects, variables, class information and method execution details.

The main memory areas are:

| Area | What it stores | Shared or per thread | Cleaned by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heap | Objects and instance variables | Shared by all threads | Garbage Collector |
| Stack | Method frames, local primitives, local references | Each thread has its own | Automatically, when the method ends |
| Metaspace | Class metadata | Shared | GC, when classes are unloaded |
| Native memory | Thread stacks, direct buffers, JIT code cache, JNI | Outside the Java heap | Not managed by the heap GC |

![Java memory areas](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/ZJEiBvtrIg6aeuYmppA0ViDlagfYSOMd92IaCnb9ZXkjhuaQAAnejBf41uVWSy8u9DnjnXwTblNwGCaZMsBTjHGWlGL89bV5B4IvzEWeG8MP13LzWFp9Q9AkmnHhwWKHPPtt-mgLG9PDz8x-RdBFQHB4wy8Np-63JYWgdA_fULmoNIpiqjQel8TXqrqpX8tY?purpose=fullsize)

```text
                    JVM Memory
                        │
     ┌──────────────────┼───────────────────┐
     ▼                  ▼                   ▼
  Heap (shared)    Per-thread areas     Outside the heap
  ├ Young Gen      ├ Stack              ├ Metaspace
  └ Old Gen        ├ PC register        ├ Thread stacks
                   └ Native method      ├ Direct buffers
                      stack             └ JIT code cache
```

### 1. Heap Memory

Heap memory is used to store objects and instance variables.

- Shared across all threads.
- Objects created using `new` are generally stored in the heap.
- Managed by the Garbage Collector.
- Divided into Young Generation and Old Generation. New objects start in the Young Generation, and long-living objects move to the Old Generation.

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Employee emp = new Employee();
    }
}
```

**What happens internally?**

1. The JVM creates the `Employee` object in Heap memory.
2. The reference variable `emp` is stored in Stack memory, because it is a local variable.
3. `emp` points to the `Employee` object in the heap.

```text
Stack                         Heap
┌──────────────┐             ┌──────────────────┐
│ emp  ────────┼───────────► │ Employee object  │
└──────────────┘             └──────────────────┘
```

![Heap and Stack](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/AN14yTYt3XbQ_ToYC5s4O71rIum6Z1zmFYUom2QveWC6YFzNk46fJwSp0689cCa-OEnGA0xQYcLz8eIzx85Ufl1ShaQcpl5Hk_xvO1h7NrbvG0Q-8SqQ7FmLfXLYQk8Ikq8M3tfgjbTfHNy7Q6ZG-5eHJvzLvkhGiU8XU3AhxdNz8E2FkeD6h9m4gfQFWgd4?purpose=fullsize)

Heap size can be set with `-Xms` (initial) and `-Xmx` (maximum), for example `-Xms512m -Xmx2g`.

### 2. Stack Memory

Stack memory stores method execution information.

- Each thread has its own stack.
- Stores local primitive variables and local object references.
- Stores method call frames.
- Memory is released automatically when the method finishes.

```java
public void calculate() {
    int a = 10;
    int b = 20;

    Employee emp = new Employee();
}
```

| Variable | Location |
| --- | --- |
| `a = 10` | Stack |
| `b = 20` | Stack |
| `emp` reference | Stack |
| `Employee` object | Heap |

Every method call creates a stack frame. When the method finishes, its frame is removed.

**What is StackOverflowError?**

Suppose a method keeps calling itself without a termination condition:

```java
public void test() {
    test();
}
```

Every call creates another stack frame. Eventually the thread's stack is exhausted, and the JVM throws:

```text
java.lang.StackOverflowError
```

**Interview answer:** `StackOverflowError` occurs when a thread's stack memory is exhausted, generally because of deep or infinite recursion. The stack size per thread can be changed with `-Xss`, but the real fix is to correct the recursion.

### 3. Where are String objects stored?

Strings are objects, so they are stored in the heap. Inside the heap, Java has a special area called the String Constant Pool (SCP).

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        String s1 = "Java";
        String s2 = "Java";

        String s3 = new String("Java");
    }
}
```

**Case 1: string literals**

```java
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Java";
```

- The JVM checks the String Constant Pool.
- For the first literal, `"Java"` is created in the pool.
- For the second, the JVM reuses the existing pooled String.
- Both references point to the same object.

```java
System.out.println(s1 == s2); // true
```

**Case 2: using new**

```java
String s3 = new String("Java");
```

- A new String object is created explicitly in the heap.
- It is separate from the pooled object.
- `s3` points to this new object.

```java
System.out.println(s1 == s3);      // false
System.out.println(s1.equals(s3)); // true
```

```text
Stack                  Heap
┌────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ s1 ────┼───┐     │  String Constant Pool        │
│ s2 ────┼───┴───► │  "Java"                      │
│ s3 ────┼───┐     ├──────────────────────────────┤
└────────┘   └───► │  "Java" (separate, via new)  │
                   └──────────────────────────────┘
```

![String Constant Pool](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/_pv_RR_FLJPxO4HfQ5rcvy_G64ZoJ1xYUEBZmJkDVWPwMyQNpYTO343LpHJRwPnGoOZ5whS8Hh3gtgtlDTu0LbvCbPKK7nqdTYCSLR4T8gxwAwYEv6urXxzcR03Z7A44tOK4-WgWXKgzZLzSF0KwH81VxvnotHPPYcO7XpN7PaNWeAuTNPZrvknuooMBRxpe?purpose=fullsize)

Remember:

- String literals are stored in the String Constant Pool.
- `new String()` explicitly creates a separate object in the heap.
- String objects are immutable.
- `==` compares references, `equals()` compares content. `s3.intern()` returns the pooled object, so `s1 == s3.intern()` is `true`.

### 4. What happens when we create an object using new?

```java
Employee emp = new Employee();
```

The JVM performs these steps:

1. Loads the `Employee` class, if it is not already loaded.
2. Allocates memory for the object in the heap.
3. Initializes instance variables with default values (`0`, `false`, `null`).
4. Executes the constructor (instance initializers run first).
5. Returns the object reference.
6. Stores that reference in the local variable `emp` in the stack (assuming it is a local variable).

![Object creation](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/La42bNn6ZX4jiT4YQTeT56LwmOnTPNFOpCzbNcY5v0aDHcgVMf5yFC068PAYzsOcq4eBTGFo5nPWwtPvdtDIQUvGlAHL7VOZ2SoxCTMDO5IA4UZBH7V5lxAUwBas58URaTbNPd5BZTqBnbXEu0st1WGH8_mJehevPIIAgCO7QoyhFEOl9w-PFrtU4YZkeM7F?purpose=fullsize)

### 5. What is a Memory Leak in Java?

A memory leak occurs when objects are no longer needed by the application, but they are still reachable through references. Because they are reachable, the Garbage Collector cannot remove them.

```java
class Main {
    static List<Object> list = new ArrayList<>();

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        while (true) {
            list.add(new Employee());
        }
    }
}
```

Here:

- Every iteration creates a new `Employee` object in the heap.
- The static list keeps a reference to every object.
- Even if they are no longer useful, they remain reachable.
- The GC cannot collect them.
- Eventually the heap is exhausted, and the JVM throws `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`.

In real projects, leaks are slower and less obvious. Typical causes:

- A static collection or cache that keeps growing and never removes entries.
- Listeners or callbacks that are registered but never removed.
- `ThreadLocal` values not removed in thread pools.
- Resources like connections, streams and statements that are not closed.

**How to prevent memory leaks**

- Remove unused objects from collections.
- Close database connections and other resources, preferably with try-with-resources.
- Avoid unnecessary static references.
- Use a cache with an eviction policy (size limit or time-to-live).
- Monitor memory usage.

### 6. What is OutOfMemoryError?

`OutOfMemoryError` occurs when the JVM cannot allocate the memory it needs, and the GC cannot free enough.

```java
List<byte[]> list = new ArrayList<>();

while (true) {
    list.add(new byte[1024 * 1024]);
}
```

Here we keep allocating 1 MB arrays in the heap until it is exhausted. The JVM throws:

```text
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
```

The message after `OutOfMemoryError:` tells us which area ran out. Sections 7 to 9 cover the other common ones.

### 7. Metaspace Exhaustion

**What is Metaspace?**

Metaspace stores class metadata, such as:

- Class structure and information.
- Method metadata.
- Runtime constant pool.
- Field and method information.

It uses native memory, not the Java heap. (Before Java 8 this was called PermGen, which was inside the heap area. Java 8 replaced it with Metaspace.)

**Example**

Suppose an application keeps loading dynamically generated classes using custom class loaders.

```java
List<ClassLoader> loaders = new ArrayList<>();

while (true) {
    ClassLoader loader = new CustomClassLoader();
    loader.loadClass("com.example.Employee");
    loaders.add(loader);   // loader stays reachable
}
```

If the classes and their class loaders stay reachable, the JVM cannot unload them. Eventually Metaspace is exhausted, and the JVM throws:

```text
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
```

**How to control Metaspace**

```text
-XX:MetaspaceSize=128m
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m
```

- `MetaspaceSize`: the initial threshold that can trigger a metadata GC.
- `MaxMetaspaceSize`: the maximum Metaspace capacity. By default it is unlimited, so Metaspace can grow until the machine runs out of native memory.

In real applications this usually shows up with repeated redeployments in an application server, or with libraries that generate many proxy or dynamic classes.

### 8. Native Memory Exhaustion

Native memory is memory allocated outside the Java heap by the JVM and native libraries. It is used for:

- Metaspace.
- Thread stacks.
- Direct ByteBuffers.
- JIT compiler code cache.
- JNI and native libraries.
- Other JVM internal structures.

**Example: DirectByteBuffer**

```java
import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<ByteBuffer> buffers = new ArrayList<>();

        while (true) {
            buffers.add(ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(10 * 1024 * 1024));
        }
    }
}
```

Here `allocateDirect()` allocates memory outside the Java heap. We keep the buffers in a list so they stay reachable. If too much direct memory is allocated, the JVM throws:

```text
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 10485760 bytes of direct buffer memory
```

(Older Java versions print `OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory`.)

**How to control direct memory**

```text
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=256m
```

By default, the limit is roughly the same as the maximum heap size.

### 9. Other common OutOfMemoryError messages

| Error message | Meaning | Usual cause | Common fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Java heap space` | Heap is full | Too many objects, or a leak | Fix the leak, increase `-Xmx` |
| `Metaspace` | Class metadata area is full | Class loader leak, too many generated classes | Fix the leak, set `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` |
| `Direct buffer memory` / `Cannot reserve ... direct buffer memory` | Direct (off-heap) memory is full | Too many direct ByteBuffers | Release buffers, set `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize` |
| `unable to create native thread` | OS cannot give more threads | Too many threads, or large thread stacks | Use thread pools, reduce `-Xss` |
| `GC overhead limit exceeded` | GC runs almost all the time and frees very little | Heap almost full, usually a leak | Fix the leak, increase heap |

### Quick summary

| Topic | One-line answer |
| --- | --- |
| Heap | Stores objects, shared, cleaned by GC |
| Stack | Per-thread method frames and local variables |
| StackOverflowError | Stack is full, usually infinite recursion |
| String Pool | Literals are reused, `new String()` creates a separate object |
| Memory leak | Unused objects are still referenced, so GC cannot remove them |
| OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space | Heap is full |
| OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace | Class metadata is full |
| OutOfMemoryError: direct buffer memory | Off-heap memory is full |

**Good to remember**

- Primitive fields inside an object live in the heap along with the object. Only local variables live on the stack.
- `StackOverflowError` and `OutOfMemoryError` are both `Error`s, not `Exception`s. We normally do not catch them.
- Calling `System.gc()` is only a request. The JVM may ignore it, and we should not depend on it.
- To find a heap problem, take a heap dump with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp` and analyze it with tools like Eclipse MAT, VisualVM or JProfiler.
- Useful tools: `jps`, `jstat`, `jmap`, `jstack` and JVisualVM.
- In containers like Docker or Kubernetes, set the heap relative to the container limit (for example `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`), because the heap is only a part of the total memory the JVM uses. Metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers also count, and if the total crosses the container limit, the container is killed with OOMKilled, even though there is no Java OutOfMemoryError.
- Our project is on Quarkus, which is mostly deployed as containers, so this container memory point is a common follow-up question.

### Interview-ready answer

Java memory is managed by the JVM. Objects and instance variables are stored in the heap, which is shared by all threads and cleaned by the Garbage Collector. Each thread has its own stack, which stores method frames, local primitives and references, and it is cleared automatically when the method ends. String literals go to the String Constant Pool inside the heap, and `new String()` creates a separate object. Class metadata is stored in Metaspace, which uses native memory. If a thread recurses without end, the stack is exhausted and we get `StackOverflowError`. If objects are no longer needed but still referenced, for example in a static collection, it is a memory leak, because the GC cannot remove them, and eventually it leads to `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. Depending on the area that runs out, we can also see `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` or an error for direct buffer memory. To diagnose it, I take a heap dump using `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and analyze it with Eclipse MAT or VisualVM.

questions.question: What is Garbage Collection in Java, and how does it work?
questions.answer:
Garbage Collection (GC) is a JVM process that automatically finds and removes objects from heap memory that the application can no longer reach.

Its main purpose is to reclaim unused memory, so the application does not run out of memory and we do not have to free memory manually like in C or C++.

### 1. How does Garbage Collection work?

The Java heap is divided into:

- Young Generation
  - Eden Space
  - Survivor S0
  - Survivor S1
- Old Generation (Tenured)

![Java heap structure](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/eFaCkGvmUHapso9tbqh1O4W0IHsc1e3akcJoIoclAQxyntw-PfGseFf7avSiBDY-49aljpiOYKyN1PQwNLtBa6j5bABOgAcFexO-rJNy-dHs5slfGJrTweXKOS_SEGFhhp9rCcIHBLRjVz97M6pj353v3_lhY8ZIz87IbEZ5j0YFtel0WOUpxH8fv3JBAIqo?purpose=fullsize)

```text
                    Java Heap
                        │
        ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
        ▼                                ▼
  Young Generation                 Old Generation
  ┌────────┬─────┬─────┐          (long-lived objects)
  │  Eden  │ S0  │ S1  │
  └────────┴─────┴─────┘
  (new objects)  (survivors)
```

Let's understand with an example:

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Employee emp1 = new Employee();
        Employee emp2 = new Employee();

        emp1 = null;
        emp2 = null;
    }
}
```

**What happens internally?**

1. Two `Employee` objects are created in heap memory.
2. Initially, `emp1` and `emp2` refer to those objects.
3. When both references become `null`, the objects become eligible for Garbage Collection (assuming no other references exist).
4. The GC identifies the unreachable objects.
5. Their memory can then be reclaimed.

**Important:** GC does not remove the objects immediately when they become unreachable. It runs according to the JVM's garbage collection strategy.

### 2. Object life cycle in the heap

```text
new Employee()
      ↓
   Eden Space
      ↓  (Eden is full -> Minor GC)
  Unreachable? ── Yes → removed
      │
      No
      ↓
  Survivor space (S0 / S1), age increases with each Minor GC
      ↓  (age crosses the threshold)
  Old Generation
```

### 3. What is Minor GC?

Minor GC is the garbage collection that mainly collects objects from the Young Generation.

```java
Employee emp1 = new Employee();
Employee emp2 = new Employee();
Employee emp3 = new Employee();
```

These objects are generally allocated in Eden Space. When Eden becomes full, a Young Generation collection happens.

- Unreachable objects are removed.
- Surviving objects are moved to a Survivor space.
- Objects that survive several collection cycles may be promoted to the Old Generation.

### 4. What is Major GC?

Major GC traditionally means garbage collection of the Old Generation.

Suppose objects survive several Young Generation collections and get promoted to the Old Generation. Eventually, the Old Generation also needs to be cleaned. Major GC reclaims the eligible objects from the Old Generation.

**Note:** The exact terms and behaviour depend on the garbage collector. For example, G1 GC uses regions and mixed collections instead of a simple fixed Young and Old collection model.

### 5. Minor GC vs Major GC

| Feature | Minor GC | Major GC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory area | Young Generation | Old Generation |
| Objects | Newly created objects | Long-lived objects |
| Frequency | Generally more frequent | Generally less frequent |
| Duration | Usually shorter | Can take longer |
| Purpose | Remove short-lived objects | Reclaim Old Generation memory |

There is also a **Full GC**, which collects the whole heap (Young and Old) and usually the Metaspace too. It is the most expensive one, and frequent Full GCs are a warning sign of a memory problem.

### 6. Can we force Garbage Collection?

We can only request it, using:

```java
System.gc();
```

or:

```java
Runtime.getRuntime().gc();
```

```java
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Employee emp = new Employee();

        emp = null;

        System.gc();

        System.out.println("GC requested");
    }
}
```

Important interview points:

- `System.gc()` only requests garbage collection.
- It does not guarantee that GC will run immediately.
- The JVM decides when to perform garbage collection.
- We should not call `System.gc()` in production applications without a specific reason. It can trigger an expensive Full GC and pause the application.

### 7. How does the JVM identify objects eligible for GC?

The JVM mainly uses **reachability analysis**. It starts from the GC Roots, such as:

- Local variables and references in the stacks of active threads.
- Static references.
- Active threads.
- JNI references.

If an object cannot be reached from any GC Root, it becomes eligible for garbage collection.

![GC Roots and reachability](https://images.openai.com/static-rsc-4/XW2Q37Js9GZKqtDnvAz0l0METobuArildKdLWLvPJuB3R6hVot38tskuUwpzcsAY4UlTtWDWc2omnOmFkFv3-U0DUGYXh0Yi7Z9dkUXsmJS0s21dTfNLpsJFywt-CBv4NvFiHx3K9mlV2OkOZBMbHdXvf3G-4nft6XQKbli8lEfSj9-k8g5OkAx7LTEV8EQC?purpose=fullsize)

```text
GC Roots (stack, static, threads)
      │
      ├──► Object A ──► Object B      reachable, stays
      │
      └──► Object C                   reachable, stays

      Object D ──► Object E           not reachable from any root,
                                      eligible for GC (even though D and E
                                      refer to each other)
```

Because of this, a group of objects that only refer to each other (a cycle) is still collected when nothing outside reaches them.

### 8. Common garbage collectors

| Collector | Flag | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Serial GC | `-XX:+UseSerialGC` | Single thread, for small applications |
| Parallel GC | `-XX:+UseParallelGC` | Multiple threads, focus on throughput |
| G1 GC | `-XX:+UseG1GC` | Default since Java 9. Region based, balances pause time and throughput |
| ZGC | `-XX:+UseZGC` | Very low pause times, for large heaps. Generational mode available from Java 21 |
| Shenandoah | `-XX:+UseShenandoahGC` | Low pause times, available in many OpenJDK builds |

Useful tuning flags:

```text
-Xms512m -Xmx2g          initial and maximum heap size
-Xlog:gc                 print GC logs (Java 9+)
```

**Good to remember**

- GC cleans only heap memory. Stack memory is released automatically when the method ends, and Metaspace is cleaned only when classes are unloaded.
- Most GC algorithms have "stop-the-world" pauses, where all application threads are paused for a short time. Newer collectors like G1, ZGC and Shenandoah try to keep these pauses small.
- GC removes only unreachable objects. If we keep objects reachable by mistake, for example in a static list or a cache that never clears, it is a memory leak and the GC cannot help. See the Java memory management entry.
- Setting a reference to `null` makes the object eligible for GC only if there are no other references to it.
- `finalize()` is deprecated for removal. Do not depend on it for cleanup. Use try-with-resources and `AutoCloseable` for resources like connections and streams.
- Reference types: strong references are never collected while reachable. `SoftReference` is cleared when memory is low (good for caches). `WeakReference` is cleared at the next GC. Prefer `WeakHashMap` or a proper cache library over hand-made caches.
- To check GC behaviour in a running application, use GC logs (`-Xlog:gc`), `jstat -gc <pid>`, VisualVM, or Actuator metrics like `jvm.gc.pause` in Spring Boot.
- Frequent Full GC, long pauses or `OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded` usually point to a memory leak or a heap that is too small.
- Our project is on Quarkus, which usually runs as containers. In containers, set the heap relative to the container limit (for example `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`) and check the GC logs when the pods show high memory.

### Interview-ready answer

Garbage Collection is the automatic memory management process in the JVM. It finds objects that are no longer reachable from the GC Roots and reclaims their heap memory, so we do not free memory manually. The heap is divided into the Young Generation, with Eden and two Survivor spaces, and the Old Generation. New objects are generally created in Eden. When Eden is full, a Minor GC removes the unreachable objects and moves the survivors to a Survivor space, and objects that survive several cycles are promoted to the Old Generation. Major GC traditionally means collecting the Old Generation, and a Full GC collects the whole heap. The exact behaviour depends on the collector, for example G1, which is the default from Java 9, uses regions instead of a fixed Young and Old split. We can request GC with `System.gc()`, but the JVM does not guarantee it, so we should not call it in production. If I see frequent Full GCs or `OutOfMemoryError`, I check GC logs and take a heap dump to look for a memory leak.

questions.question: What are the SOLID principles? Explain each with an example.
What are the main features of Java 8.
questions.answer:
Java 8 is a major release. For interviews, remember these main features:

```text
Java 8
│
├── 1. Lambda Expressions
├── 2. Functional Interfaces
├── 3. Stream API
├── 4. Optional
├── 5. forEach()
├── 6. Collectors
└── 7. CompletableFuture
```

| # | Feature | In one line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Lambda Expressions | A short way to pass behavior (a function) without an anonymous class |
| 2 | Functional Interfaces | Interfaces with exactly one abstract method; lambdas implement them |
| 3 | Stream API | Declarative processing of collections: filter, map, sorted, collect |
| 4 | Optional | A container that makes a possibly-missing value explicit |
| 5 | forEach() | Iterate a collection with a lambda or method reference |
| 6 | Collectors | Collect stream results into a List, Set, Map and more |
| 7 | CompletableFuture | Asynchronous programming without blocking the current thread |

### 1. Lambda Expressions ⭐

Before Java 8, if we wanted to pass behavior, we commonly used anonymous classes.

**Before Java 8**

```java
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Rahul", "Amit", "John");

Collections.sort(names, new Comparator<String>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        return a.compareTo(b);
    }
});
```

That's quite verbose.

**Java 8**

```java
Collections.sort(names, (a, b) -> a.compareTo(b));
```

The `(a, b) -> a.compareTo(b)` is a lambda expression.

**Simple definition**

A lambda expression allows us to represent a function/behavior in a concise way without creating an anonymous class.

General syntax:

```text
(parameters) -> expression
```

or:

```text
(parameters) -> {
    // statements
}
```

Example:

```java
(a, b) -> a + b
```

### 2. Functional Interface ⭐

A functional interface is an interface that has exactly one abstract method.

Example:

```java
@FunctionalInterface
interface Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b);
}
```

Now we can use a lambda:

```java
Calculator calculator = (a, b) -> a + b;

System.out.println(calculator.add(10, 20));
```

Output:

```text
30
```

Java provides many built-in functional interfaces:

| Interface | Method | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Predicate<T>` | `test(T)` | Takes a value, returns `true` or `false` |
| `Function<T, R>` | `apply(T)` | Takes a value, returns a result |
| `Consumer<T>` | `accept(T)` | Takes a value, returns nothing |
| `Supplier<T>` | `get()` | Takes nothing, returns a value |
| `UnaryOperator<T>` | `apply(T)` | Takes a value, returns the same type |
| `BinaryOperator<T>` | `apply(T, T)` | Takes two values of one type, returns that type |

For example:

```java
Predicate<Integer> p = x -> x > 10;

System.out.println(p.test(20)); // true
```

### 3. Stream API ⭐⭐⭐

This is one of the most important Java 8 features for interviews.

Streams allow us to process collections in a more declarative way.

Suppose:

```java
List<Integer> numbers =
        Arrays.asList(10, 15, 20, 25, 30);
```

We want numbers greater than 20.

**Traditional approach**

```java
for (Integer number : numbers) {
    if (number > 20) {
        System.out.println(number);
    }
}
```

**Java 8 Stream**

```java
numbers.stream()
       .filter(n -> n > 20)
       .forEach(System.out::println);
```

Output:

```text
25
30
```

Stream operations can be thought of as:

```text
Collection
    ↓
 stream()
    ↓
 filter()
    ↓
 map()
    ↓
 sorted()
    ↓
 collect()
```

Operations like `filter()`, `map()` and `sorted()` are intermediate operations. They only run when a terminal operation such as `forEach()` or `collect()` is called. A stream does not modify the original collection.

### 4. Optional ⭐

Optional was introduced to provide a better way of representing a value that may or may not be present.

Without Optional:

```java
String name = getName();

if (name != null) {
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

With Optional:

```java
Optional<String> name = Optional.ofNullable(getName());

name.ifPresent(System.out::println);
```

You can also provide a default:

```java
String result = Optional.ofNullable(getName())
        .orElse("Unknown");
```

So:

```text
Optional
    ↓
Value exists? ── Yes → use value
       │
       No
       ↓
   default value
```

It helps make absence of a value explicit, although Optional is not a guarantee that all null-related problems disappear.

### 5. forEach()

Java 8 added `forEach()` to `Iterable`.

Instead of:

```java
for (String name : names) {
    System.out.println(name);
}
```

you can write:

```java
names.forEach(name -> System.out.println(name));
```

or:

```java
names.forEach(System.out::println);
```

`System.out::println` is a method reference, a shorter form of the lambda `name -> System.out.println(name)`.

### 6. Collectors

Collectors is heavily used with Streams.

For example:

```java
List<String> result = names.stream()
        .filter(name -> name.length() > 4)
        .collect(Collectors.toList());
```

You can also create maps:

```java
Map<Integer, String> map = employees.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(
                Employee::getId,
                Employee::getName
        ));
```

Other commonly used collectors:

| Collector | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `Collectors.toList()` | Collects elements into a List |
| `Collectors.toSet()` | Collects elements into a Set |
| `Collectors.toMap()` | Collects elements into a Map |
| `Collectors.groupingBy()` | Groups elements by a key |
| `Collectors.partitioningBy()` | Splits elements into two groups: true and false |
| `Collectors.joining()` | Joins strings into one string |
| `Collectors.counting()` | Counts the elements |

### 7. CompletableFuture

Java 8 introduced `CompletableFuture` for asynchronous programming.

Example:

```java
CompletableFuture<String> future =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Hello");

future.thenAccept(System.out::println);
```

Conceptually:

```text
Main Thread
    │
    ├──── start async task ────► Another thread
    │                                │
    │                                ▼
    │                          process operation
    │                                │
    ◄──────────── result ────────────┘
```

This is useful when we don't want the current thread to block while waiting for some asynchronous operation.

**Also worth knowing:** Java 8 also added default and static methods in interfaces, and the new Date and Time API (`java.time`).

questions.question: What is the difference between Future and CompletableFuture in Java?
questions.answer:
Both `Future` and `CompletableFuture` are used to handle asynchronous operations in Java, but `CompletableFuture` gives us many more features. In simple words, `Future` lets us start a task and wait for its result, while `CompletableFuture` lets us say what should happen after the result comes, without waiting.

```text
Future:             start task -> wait (blocked) -> get result -> do next step

CompletableFuture:  start task -> register next steps (thenApply, thenAccept...) -> thread is free
                                       ... result arrives -> next steps run automatically
```

### 1. Future

`Future` was introduced in Java 5. It represents the result of an asynchronous computation that may be available in the future.

Main features:

- Submit tasks asynchronously using `ExecutorService`.
- Get the result using `get()`.
- Check if the task is completed using `isDone()`.
- Cancel the task using `cancel()`.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        ExecutorService executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();

        Future<Integer> future = executor.submit(() -> {
            Thread.sleep(2000);
            return 100;
        });

        Integer result = future.get();   // blocks here for about 2 seconds

        System.out.println(result);

        executor.shutdown();
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
100
```

**Limitations of Future**

- `get()` is blocking. The calling thread waits until the result is available.
- We cannot chain steps, like "when the result comes, then do this".
- There is no callback support.
- We cannot combine two futures directly.
- Exception handling is limited. `get()` throws checked exceptions (`InterruptedException`, `ExecutionException`).
- We cannot complete it manually.

### 2. CompletableFuture

`CompletableFuture` was introduced in Java 8. It supports asynchronous programming and lets us chain multiple operations without blocking the calling thread. It implements the `Future` interface, so everything `Future` can do, it can do too.

Main features:

- Non-blocking execution.
- Chain multiple operations.
- Combine multiple asynchronous tasks.
- Handle exceptions.
- Complete a future manually.

```java
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 100)
                .thenApply(result -> result * 2)
                .thenAccept(System.out::println)
                .join();
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
200
```

Here:

- `supplyAsync()` runs the task asynchronously.
- `thenApply()` transforms the result.
- `thenAccept()` uses the result and returns nothing.
- `join()` is added only in this small demo. The async tasks run on daemon threads, so if `main` ends first, the JVM can exit before `200` is printed.

### 3. Difference between Future and CompletableFuture

| Feature | Future | CompletableFuture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Introduced | Java 5 | Java 8 |
| Asynchronous execution | Yes | Yes |
| Non-blocking chaining | No | Yes |
| `get()` | Blocking | Also available and also blocking. Use `join()` or callbacks |
| Exception handling | Limited, only through `get()` | `exceptionally()`, `handle()`, `whenComplete()` |
| Combine tasks | Not directly | `thenCombine()`, `allOf()`, `anyOf()` |
| Manual completion | No | `complete()`, `completeExceptionally()` |
| Callback support | No | Yes (`thenApply`, `thenAccept`, `thenRun`) |
| Timeout | Only `get(timeout, unit)`, which blocks | `orTimeout()`, `completeOnTimeout()` (Java 9+) |
| Custom thread pool | Decided when we call `submit()` | Pass an executor to `supplyAsync(task, executor)` |

### 4. Important CompletableFuture methods

| Method | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `supplyAsync()` | Runs an async task and returns a result |
| `runAsync()` | Runs an async task without returning a result |
| `thenApply()` | Transforms the result |
| `thenAccept()` | Uses the result, returns nothing |
| `thenRun()` | Runs the next task without receiving the result |
| `thenCompose()` | Chains a dependent asynchronous operation |
| `thenCombine()` | Combines two independent results |
| `allOf()` | Waits for all futures to complete |
| `anyOf()` | Completes when any one future completes |
| `exceptionally()` | Handles an exception and gives a fallback value |
| `handle()` | Handles both success and failure |

### 5. Practical Spring Boot example

Suppose we have an e-commerce application. We need to fetch:

- User details from User Service
- Product details from Product Service
- Order details from Order Service

```java
CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> userService.getUser());

CompletableFuture<Product> productFuture =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> productService.getProduct());

CompletableFuture<Order> orderFuture =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderService.getOrder());

CompletableFuture.allOf(userFuture, productFuture, orderFuture).join();

User user = userFuture.join();
Product product = productFuture.join();
Order order = orderFuture.join();
```

All three independent service calls run at the same time, instead of waiting for one another. If each takes 2 seconds, the total is about 2 seconds, not 6.

**The same thing with plain Future**

With `Future`, we can also start the three calls together, but we have to call `get()` on each one, and each `get()` blocks the thread. There is no way to say "when all are done" or "if one fails, use a fallback" without writing extra code.

```java
Future<User> userFuture = executor.submit(() -> userService.getUser());
Future<Product> productFuture = executor.submit(() -> productService.getProduct());

User user = userFuture.get();        // blocks
Product product = productFuture.get();  // blocks
```

For the fallback part, see the earlier entry on `CompletableFuture` with `exceptionally()`.

### 6. thenApply() vs thenCompose() vs thenCombine()

This is a very common interview question.

| Method | Purpose | Simple way to remember |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `thenApply()` | Transforms a result | Like `map()` |
| `thenCompose()` | Chains another asynchronous operation | Like `flatMap()` |
| `thenCombine()` | Combines two independent asynchronous results | Wait for both, then merge |

**thenApply: simple transformation**

```java
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 10)
        .thenApply(n -> n * 2)
        .thenAccept(System.out::println)
        .join();
```

Output:

```text
20
```

**thenCompose: the next step is itself async**

First we get the user, then we use that user to fetch the orders. The second call needs the output of the first, so they cannot run in parallel.

```java
CompletableFuture<List<Order>> orders =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> userService.getUser(101))
                .thenCompose(user ->
                        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderService.getOrders(user)));
```

If we used `thenApply()` here, the result would be a `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<List<Order>>>`, which is nested. `thenCompose()` flattens it.

**thenCombine: two independent calls, merge the results**

```java
CompletableFuture<Integer> price =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 1000);

CompletableFuture<Integer> discount =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 100);

int finalPrice = price
        .thenCombine(discount, (p, d) -> p - d)
        .join();

System.out.println(finalPrice);   // 900
```

### Quick summary

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Just run a task and wait for the result | `Future` |
| Run a task and do something after, without blocking | `CompletableFuture` with `thenApply` / `thenAccept` |
| Next call depends on the previous result | `thenCompose()` |
| Two independent calls, merge the results | `thenCombine()` |
| Many independent calls, wait for all | `allOf()` |
| Handle failure with a fallback | `exceptionally()` or `handle()` |

**Good to remember**

- `CompletableFuture.get()` is still blocking. The non-blocking part is the chaining with `thenApply`, `thenAccept` and others. Calling `join()` or `get()` at the end blocks the thread, which is fine at the very end of a flow, but not in the middle.
- `join()` throws an unchecked `CompletionException`, while `get()` throws checked exceptions. `join()` is easier inside lambdas and streams.
- `supplyAsync()` without an executor uses the common ForkJoinPool. For blocking calls like HTTP or database, pass your own executor: `supplyAsync(task, executor)`.
- `thenApply()` and `thenApplyAsync()` are different. The plain one may run on the same thread that completed the previous step. The `Async` version runs the step on a pool thread.
- `allOf()` returns `CompletableFuture<Void>`, so it gives no results. We read each result from the individual futures.
- Cancelling a `CompletableFuture` does not interrupt the running thread. It only completes the future with a `CancellationException`.
- `CompletableFuture` is not reactive streaming. It handles one value. For a stream of values, we use `Flux` from WebFlux.
- With Java 21 virtual threads, simple blocking code can sometimes replace complex `CompletableFuture` chains. `CompletableFuture` is still useful when we need to combine results and handle failures in a flow.
- Our project is on Quarkus, where the similar tools are `Uni` and `Multi` from Mutiny, and `CompletionStage` in the REST layer.

### Interview-ready answer

Both `Future` and `CompletableFuture` are used for asynchronous operations. `Future` was introduced in Java 5, and it represents the result of a task that will be available later. We submit a task with `ExecutorService` and read the result with `get()`, but `get()` blocks the calling thread, and we cannot chain steps, add callbacks or combine tasks easily. `CompletableFuture` was introduced in Java 8 and it implements `Future`, but it adds non-blocking chaining with methods like `thenApply()` and `thenAccept()`, combining tasks with `thenCombine()` and `allOf()`, exception handling with `exceptionally()` and `handle()`, and manual completion. For example, in an e-commerce application, I call User, Product and Order services using `supplyAsync()`, wait for all with `allOf()`, and then collect the results, so the total time is the slowest call and not the sum of all. I use `thenApply()` to transform a result, `thenCompose()` when the next call depends on the previous result, and `thenCombine()` when I have two independent results to merge.

questions.answer:
Tight Coupling: When one class or service is highly dependent on another, it is tightly coupled. If we change one component, it can cause problems.

Problems:

- Difficult to test and maintain.
- Difficult to replace implementation.
- Changes can impact multiple components.
- Less flexibility.

```java
class EmailService {

        System.out.println("Sending Email");
    }
}

class NotificationService {

    private EmailService emailService = new EmailService();

    public void notifyUser() {

    }
}
```

```text
        ↓
   EmailService
```

NotificationService is tightly coupled to EmailService.

**What happens if we want SMS?**

Suppose tomorrow we want:

- Email
- SMS
- WhatsApp

We need to modify NotificationService because it specifically creates:

`new EmailService()`

That's the problem.

**Why is this difficult?**

If we change `EmailService` it can affect:

```text
NotificationService
      ↓
Other classes
      ↓
Tests
```

So the components become harder to change independently.

questions.question: What are microservices, and how do services communicate with each other?
questions.answer:
Microservices is an architectural style where a large application is divided into small, independent and loosely coupled services, with each service being responsible for a specific business capability.

Each microservice is developed, deployed, scaled and maintained independently and each microservice contains their own database to maintain loose coupling.

One service can't access directly other's service database. Instead each microservice communicate through APIs or messaging system.

Mainly there are two approaches by which two or more services communicate with each other.

1. **Synchronous Communication**, where a service sends request to another service and waits for response. This is synchronous communication. For synchronous communication, microservices use REST API, HTTP, gRPC and Web Client.
2. **Asynchronous Communication**, where a service communicate each other through a message broker instead of directly waiting for each other's response. For asynchronous communication, microservices use Kafka, RabbitMQ, and Amazon SQS.

questions.question: What is the difference between a bounded and an unbounded microservice?
questions.answer:
### Bounded Microservice

A bounded microservice has a clear business responsibility and well-defined boundary. It owns its data, logic, and APIs for a specific business capability.

Example:

```text
Customer Service
└── Customer Management

Account Service
└── Account Operations

Loan Service
└── Loan Processing

Payment Service
└── Payment Processing
```

### Unbounded Microservice

An unbounded microservice has responsibilities that span multiple business domains and lacks clear boundaries.

Example:

```text
CustomerAccountLoanService
```

This service handles:

- Customer management
- Account operations
- Loan processing
- Notifications

**Note:** The idea of a bounded microservice comes from the bounded context in Domain-Driven Design (DDD). "Unbounded microservice" is an informal term. A service that mixes several domains like this is often described as a "god service" or a mini-monolith.

questions.question: Explain JPA and Hibernate in short.
questions.answer:
**JPA** is a specification that provides a set of interfaces, such as `EntityManager`, and annotations such as `@Entity`, `@OneToMany`, and `@ManyToOne` for managing persistence and mapping Java objects to database tables.

**Hibernate** is an ORM framework that implements the JPA specification. It handles actual database operations, such as generating and executing SQL queries, caching, and lazy loading.

questions.question: What is Kafka?
questions.answer:
Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used to handle high-volume, real-time data between applications and microservices.

Kafka is also used in microservices architecture for asynchronous communication between microservices and event-driven architecture.

questions.question: What are the components of Kafka?
questions.answer:
Kafka Components:

- Producer
- Consumer
- Topic
- Partition
- Consumer Group
- Broker

### 1. Producer

A Producer is an application/service that sends messages to Kafka.

Suppose Rahul places an order:

```text
Rahul
  │
  │ Buy Laptop
  ▼
Order Service
  │
  │ creates Order
  ▼
Kafka
```

The Order Service acts as the Producer.

It publishes an event:

```json
{
  "orderId": 101,
  "customerId": 5001,
  "product": "Laptop",
  "amount": 70000,
  "status": "CREATED"
}
```

In Spring Boot:

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public OrderService(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderEvent> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public void createOrder(OrderEvent event) {

        // Save order to database

        kafkaTemplate.send("order-topic", event);
    }
}
```

So:

```text
Order Service
      │
      │ Producer
      ▼
Kafka → order-topic
```

### 2. Consumer

A Consumer reads messages/events from Kafka.

Suppose Payment Service needs to process newly created orders.

```text
Kafka
  │
  │ order-topic
  ▼
Payment Service
```

Payment Service becomes the Consumer.

Spring Boot:

```java
@Service
public class PaymentConsumer {

    @KafkaListener(topics = "order-topic")
    public void consume(OrderEvent event) {

        System.out.println(
            "Received order: " + event.getOrderId()
        );

        // Process payment
    }
}
```

Now the flow is:

```text
Order Service
    │
    │ Producer
    ▼
 Kafka
    │
    │ order-topic
    ▼
Payment Service
    │
    │ Consumer
    ▼
Process Payment
```

### 3. Topic

A Topic is a logical category/name where related events are published.

For example:

- order-topic
- payment-topic
- notification-topic
- customer-topic

Our Order Service sends events to:

`order-topic`

Think of a topic like a named stream/channel.

```text
                  Kafka
                    │
       ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
       ▼            ▼             ▼
 order-topic   payment-topic   customer-topic
```

For example:

```text
order-topic
     │
     ├── OrderCreated
     ├── OrderCreated
     ├── OrderCancelled
     ├── OrderCreated
     └── OrderShipped
```

### 4. Partition

A topic is divided into partitions to provide parallel processing and scalability.

Suppose:

`order-topic`

has 3 partitions:

```text
             order-topic
                  │
        ┌─────────┼─────────┐
        ▼         ▼         ▼
   Partition 0 Partition 1 Partition 2
```

Messages are distributed among these partitions.

For example:

```text
Partition 0
----------------
Order 101
Order 104
Order 107


Partition 1
----------------
Order 102
Order 105
Order 108


Partition 2
----------------
Order 103
Order 106
Order 109
```

**Why do we do this?**

Parallel processing

Imagine we have 1 million orders.

If everything goes into one partition:

```text
1 million messages
       ↓
 One partition
       ↓
One processing path
```

That can become a bottleneck.

With multiple partitions:

```text
                 1 million events
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ▼            ▼            ▼
      Partition 0  Partition 1  Partition 2
          │            │            │
          ▼            ▼            ▼
      Consumer      Consumer      Consumer
```

Now processing can happen in parallel.

### 5. Consumer Group

A group of message consumers working together to process messages.

Now let's make the system bigger.

Suppose Payment Service needs 3 instances because there are lots of orders.

```text
              order-topic
                   │
             Consumer Group
                   │
       ┌───────────┼───────────┐
       ▼           ▼           ▼
 Payment-1     Payment-2    Payment-3
```

These three consumers belong to the same:

`payment-service-group`

They work together.

For example:

```text
Partition 0 ──────► Payment-1

Partition 1 ──────► Payment-2

Partition 2 ──────► Payment-3
```

So the workload is distributed.

**Very important rule**

Within one consumer group, one partition is consumed by only one consumer at a time.

For example:

```text
Topic: order-topic

P0 ─────────► Consumer 1
P1 ─────────► Consumer 2
P2 ─────────► Consumer 3
```

This prevents the same partition's messages from being processed simultaneously by multiple consumers in that group.

### 6. Broker

A Kafka server that stores and serves messages. A Kafka cluster normally contains multiple brokers for scalability and fault tolerance.

A Broker is a Kafka server.

A Kafka system normally has multiple brokers.

For example:

```text
                 Kafka Cluster

        ┌──────────┐
        │ Broker 1 │
        └──────────┘

        ┌──────────┐
        │ Broker 2 │
        └──────────┘

        ┌──────────┐
        │ Broker 3 │
        └──────────┘
```

Kafka distributes partitions across brokers.

For example:

```text
                 order-topic

        ┌────────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
        │            │            │
        ▼            ▼            ▼
    Partition 0  Partition 1  Partition 2
        │            │            │
        ▼            ▼            ▼
     Broker 1     Broker 2     Broker 3
```

This helps Kafka scale horizontally and remain available when configured with replication.

questions.question: What are the main components of Angular?
Explain Angular component lifecycle.
questions.answer:
Angular Component Lifecycle:

The lifecycle of angular component is:

```text
Component Created
      ↓
constructor()
      ↓
ngOnChanges()
      ↓
ngOnInit()
      ↓
ngDoCheck()
      ↓
ngAfterContentInit()
      ↓
ngAfterContentChecked()
      ↓
ngAfterViewInit()
      ↓
ngAfterViewChecked()
      ↓
  Component Updates
      ↓
ngOnChanges() / ngDoCheck()
      ↓
...
      ↓
ngOnDestroy()
```

### 1. constructor()

I generally avoid putting API calls or complex initialization logic here.

```typescript
constructor(private userService: UserService) {}
```

### 2. ngOnChanges()

Called when an `@Input()` property receives a value or changes.

```typescript
@Input() userId!: number;

ngOnChanges(changes: SimpleChanges) {
  console.log('Input changed', changes);
}
```

### 3. ngOnInit()

Called once after Angular initializes the component's inputs.

```typescript
ngOnInit() {
  this.loadUsers();
}
```

### 4. ngDoCheck()

Called during Angular's change-detection cycle.

```typescript
ngDoCheck() {
  // custom change detection logic
}
```

### 5. ngAfterContentInit()

Called once after Angular projects external content into the component using:

```html
<ng-content></ng-content>
```

### 6. ngAfterContentChecked()

Called after Angular checks the projected content. Because it can run frequently during change detection, it should be used carefully.

### 7. ngAfterViewInit()

Called once after the component's view and child views are initialized.

This is useful when you need access to:

- DOM elements
- `@ViewChild`
- Child components

### 8. ngAfterViewChecked()

Called after Angular checks the component's view and child views.

### 9. ngOnDestroy()

Called immediately before Angular destroys the component. This is very important in real-world applications for cleanup.

```typescript
ngOnDestroy() {
  this.subscription.unsubscribe();
}
```

questions.question: How do you remove duplicates from a list, sort it in descending order, and place odd numbers before even numbers using Java Streams?
questions.answer:
```java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<Integer> list = List.of(1, 2, 4, 2, 3, 7, 9, 3, 15, 12, 45);

        List<Integer> result = list.stream()
                .distinct()
                .sorted(
                        Comparator.comparingInt((Integer n) -> n % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 0)
                                .thenComparing(Comparator.reverseOrder())
                )
                .collect(Collectors.toList());

        for (int n : result) {
            System.out.println(" " + n);
        }
    }
}
```

Output:

```text
 45
 15
 9
 7
 3
 1
 12
 4
 2
```

**How it works**

1. `distinct()` removes duplicates, so `[1, 2, 4, 2, 3, 7, 9, 3, 15, 12, 45]` becomes `[1, 2, 4, 3, 7, 9, 15, 12, 45]`.
2. `Comparator.comparingInt(n -> n % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 0)` gives each number a key: odd numbers get `0`, even numbers get `1`. Sorting is ascending by key, so all odd numbers come before all even numbers.
3. `thenComparing(Comparator.reverseOrder())` is the tie-breaker. Numbers with the same key (both odd or both even) are sorted in descending order.
4. `collect(Collectors.toList())` gathers the result into a new list.

So the two groups are sorted separately:

```text
Odd  group: 1, 3, 7, 9, 15, 45  -> 45, 15, 9, 7, 3, 1
Even group: 2, 4, 12            -> 12, 4, 2
```

Final result: `45, 15, 9, 7, 3, 1, 12, 4, 2`.

**Notes**

- The result is not one single descending list. It is odd numbers in descending order, followed by even numbers in descending order. If the interviewer wants plain descending order, use only `.sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())`.
- `(Integer n)` in the lambda is needed so Java can infer the type when you chain `thenComparing(...)` after `comparingInt(...)`.
- Use `n % 2 == 0` rather than `n % 2 == 1` for the check. For negative odd numbers, `n % 2` gives `-1`, so a `== 1` check would treat them as even.
- `System.out.println(" " + n)` prints each number on its own line. Use `System.out.print(n + " ")` to print them on one line.

**Complexity**

- Time: O(n log n), because of sorting.
- Space: O(n), for the distinct list and the result.

questions.question: What is the Java Stream API, and what are its three steps?
questions.answer:
Instead of writing traditional `while`, `for` and `do-while` loops, Java 8 introduced the Stream API. We just say what we want to do with the data (filter, convert, count), and Java takes care of the looping. It does not change the original collection.

Every stream pipeline has three steps:

```text
Source  ->  Intermediate operations  ->  Terminal operation
```

```java
List<String> names = List.of("Rahul", "Amit", "Vikas", "Anil");

List<String> result = names.stream()                      // 1. Source
        .filter(n -> n.startsWith("A"))                  // 2. Intermediate
        .map(String::toUpperCase)                        // 2. Intermediate
        .collect(Collectors.toList());                   // 3. Terminal

System.out.println(result);
```

Output:

```text
[AMIT, ANIL]
```

### 1. Source

- This is where the stream starts. It gives the data to the pipeline.
- The source can be a collection, an array, a file, or even generated values.
- Creating a stream does not process anything yet. It only opens the pipeline.

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `collection.stream()` | Creates a stream from a List, Set, etc. |
| `collection.parallelStream()` | Creates a stream that can run in parallel |
| `Arrays.stream(array)` | Creates a stream from an array |
| `Stream.of(a, b, c)` | Creates a stream from the given values |
| `Stream.iterate(seed, f)` | Creates an infinite stream, each value from the previous one |
| `Stream.generate(supplier)` | Creates an infinite stream from a Supplier |
| `IntStream.range(1, 5)` | Numbers 1 to 4 (`rangeClosed(1, 5)` includes 5) |
| `str.chars()` | Stream of the characters of a String |
| `Files.lines(path)` | Stream of the lines of a file |

### 2. Intermediate Operations

- These operations transform or filter the stream and give back another stream, so we can chain many of them.
- They are lazy. Nothing runs until a terminal operation is called.
- They never change the source. They just describe what to do with each element.

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `filter(Predicate)` | Keeps only the elements that match the condition |
| `map(Function)` | Converts each element into another value |
| `flatMap(Function)` | Converts each element into a stream and merges them into one |
| `distinct()` | Removes duplicates |
| `sorted()` / `sorted(Comparator)` | Sorts the elements |
| `limit(n)` | Takes only the first n elements |
| `skip(n)` | Skips the first n elements |
| `peek(Consumer)` | Looks at each element, mostly for debugging |
| `mapToInt()` / `mapToObj()` / `boxed()` | Moves between object streams and primitive streams |

Java 9 also added `takeWhile()` and `dropWhile()`.

### 3. Terminal Operation

- This is the last step. It starts the whole pipeline and gives the final result (a list, a number, true/false, or nothing).
- A pipeline can have only one terminal operation.
- After it runs, the stream is used up. Using the same stream again throws `IllegalStateException`.

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `forEach(Consumer)` | Performs an action on each element |
| `collect(Collector)` | Gathers the result into a List, Set, Map, etc. |
| `reduce(identity, op)` | Combines all elements into one value (e.g. sum) |
| `count()` | Returns the number of elements |
| `min()` / `max()` | Returns the smallest / largest element |
| `sum()` / `average()` | Sum or average (on `IntStream`, `LongStream`, `DoubleStream`) |
| `anyMatch()` / `allMatch()` / `noneMatch()` | Checks a condition, returns true/false |
| `findFirst()` / `findAny()` | Returns one element inside an `Optional` |
| `toArray()` | Puts the elements into an array |

Java 16 also added `toList()` directly on a stream.

**Remember**

- A stream does not store data and does not modify the source collection.
- Intermediate operations are lazy, and the terminal operation triggers everything.
- A stream can be used only once.

questions.question: What are sealed classes in Java 17, and what are sealed, non-sealed and final used for?
questions.answer:
Sealed classes were introduced as a final feature in Java 17. They are used to control inheritance, by restricting which classes can extend a particular class, or which classes can implement an interface.

(They were in preview in Java 15 and 16 before becoming final in Java 17.)

We mainly use three keywords:

### 1. sealed

The parent class uses `sealed` along with `permits` to list the child classes that are allowed to extend it.

### 2. non-sealed

A permitted child class uses `non-sealed` when it wants to open up the hierarchy again, so any other class can extend it without restriction.

### 3. final

A permitted child class uses `final` when it does not want to allow any further inheritance.

**Example**

```java
public sealed class Payment
        permits UpiPayment, CardPayment, CashPayment {
}
```

Permitted child classes:

```java
public final class UpiPayment extends Payment {
}

public non-sealed class CardPayment extends Payment {
}

public sealed class CashPayment extends Payment
        permits OnlineCashPayment {
}
```

Further inheritance:

```java
public class VisaPayment extends CardPayment {
}

public final class OnlineCashPayment extends CashPayment {
}
```

(Each public class goes in its own file.)

The hierarchy looks like this:

```text
                    Payment (sealed)
                         │
      ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
      ▼                  ▼                  ▼
 UpiPayment         CardPayment        CashPayment
  (final)          (non-sealed)         (sealed)
                         │                  │
                         ▼                  ▼
                   VisaPayment     OnlineCashPayment
                (anyone can extend)       (final)
```

- `UpiPayment` is `final`, so nobody can extend it.
- `CardPayment` is `non-sealed`, so any class can extend it. That is why `VisaPayment` is allowed.
- `CashPayment` is `sealed` again, so only `OnlineCashPayment` can extend it, and that one is `final`.

**Understand the difference**

| Keyword | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `sealed` | Restricts which classes can inherit |
| `permits` | Specifies the allowed direct subclasses |
| `non-sealed` | Opens the inheritance hierarchy again |
| `final` | Stops further inheritance |

**Good to remember**

- Every permitted subclass must be declared `final`, `sealed` or `non-sealed`. If you leave all three out, the code will not compile.
- `permits` is not a separate keyword on its own. It is a clause that goes with `sealed`.
- Sealed works for interfaces too: `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}`.
- If the permitted subclasses are in the same file as the parent, you can skip `permits` and the compiler works it out.
- Permitted subclasses must be in the same module, or in the same package if you are not using modules.
- Sealed classes work nicely with pattern matching for `switch`, because the compiler knows all the possible subtypes.

How does Spring Boot auto-configuration determine which beans to create?
questions.answer:
Spring Boot auto-configuration decides which beans to create by checking four things: which dependencies are added, whether the required classes are available, whether the beans already exist, and what properties are configured.

Let's understand it with a JPA example.

### 1. We add the dependencies

In `pom.xml`, we add:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
    <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
```

Maven downloads the required libraries. For example, the JPA dependency brings classes such as `EntityManager` into the project.

### 2. We start the Spring Boot application

```java
SpringApplication.run(EmployeeApplication.class, args);
```

`@SpringBootApplication` enables three things:

- `@SpringBootConfiguration`
- `@EnableAutoConfiguration`
- `@ComponentScan`

`@EnableAutoConfiguration` is the one that switches on auto-configuration.

### 3. Spring finds our application classes

Component scanning discovers our own classes:

- `EmployeeController`
- `EmployeeService`
- `EmployeeRepository`

Spring manages the required objects. Spring Data JPA also creates an implementation for our `JpaRepository` interface, so we never write that class ourselves.

### 4. Spring Boot checks the classes on the classpath

Because we added JPA, Spring Boot finds its internal JPA auto-configuration classes. An internal configuration can have a condition like this:

```java
@ConditionalOnClass(EntityManager.class)
```

Spring Boot asks: "Is `EntityManager.class` available in the project's libraries?" We added the JPA dependency, so the class is there and the condition matches.

**Important:** it checks whether the class exists, not whether we are using it in our code.

### 5. Spring Boot checks the existing beans

Suppose it wants to create a `DataSource`. It checks:

```java
@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)
```

- If a `DataSource` bean does not exist, Spring Boot creates its default `DataSource`.
- If we already created one, Spring Boot skips its default. This is called backing off.

### 6. Spring Boot reads application.properties

```properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/employee_db
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=root
```

It uses these details to configure the database connection.

### 7. Spring Boot creates the required beans

| Bean | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `DataSource` | Manages database connections |
| `EntityManagerFactory` | Creates `EntityManager` instances |
| `TransactionManager` | Manages database transactions |

These beans are registered in the Spring `ApplicationContext` and become available for dependency injection.

**Complete process**

```text
Add dependencies in pom.xml
          ↓
Start Spring Boot application
          ↓
Discover relevant auto-configuration classes
          ↓
Check required classes and existing beans
          ↓
Read application.properties
          ↓
Create and register required beans
```

### Three annotations to remember

| Annotation | Question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| `@ConditionalOnClass` | Is the required class available? |
| `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` | Does the bean already exist? |
| `@ConditionalOnProperty` | Is the required property configured with the expected value? |

That's how Spring Boot decides which beans to create.

### Interview-ready answer

Spring Boot auto-configuration automatically determines which beans are required based on the classes available on the classpath, the existing beans and the application properties.

For example, when I add Spring Data JPA and MySQL dependencies, Spring Boot discovers the relevant JPA auto-configuration classes.

It checks whether the required classes, such as `EntityManager`, are available using `@ConditionalOnClass`. It also checks whether beans already exist using `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`.

If the conditions are satisfied, Spring Boot creates beans such as `DataSource`, `EntityManagerFactory` and `TransactionManager` and registers them in the `ApplicationContext`.

If I provide my own `DataSource` bean, Spring Boot backs off from creating its default `DataSource`.

**Good to remember**

- Our own beans are registered first, and auto-configuration runs after them. That is why `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` works and our custom bean wins.
- Auto-configuration classes are listed in a file inside the Spring Boot jars: `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (older versions used `spring.factories`). Spring Boot reads this list and evaluates the conditions on each class.
- To see which auto-configurations matched and which did not, run the app with `--debug` or `debug=true`. It prints a conditions evaluation report. In Actuator, the `/conditions` endpoint shows the same.
- To exclude an auto-configuration, use `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)`.
- With the starter, the default connection pool is HikariCP.
